title: Endocrine Biochemistry and Nutrition
subject: Endocrine System (ENDO)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter connects hormones to the biochemistry and nutrients they depend on. It explains how insulin and glucagon switch the body between storing and releasing fuel, how losing that switch produces diabetic ketoacidosis, and how iodine, selenium, vitamin D, and magnesium are built into or required by endocrine pathways. It closes with leptin and ghrelin in appetite control and the link between visceral fat and insulin resistance. Board questions typically give a lab pattern or a deficiency and ask which enzyme, hormone, or feedback step explains it, so focus on the direction of each change and why it happens.

Hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis and thyroid follicle structure (EN-3)

connections.how: Absolute insulin deficiency in type 1 diabetes produces the ketoacidosis described here, while the insulin resistance of type 2 diabetes builds on visceral adiposity.
The anion gap, bicarbonate buffering, and respiratory compensation explain the laboratory picture of ketoacidosis.
Iodine deficiency is the leading cause of goiter and hypothyroidism worldwide, and deiodinase activity decides how much active T3 tissues receive.
Vitamin D deficiency produces rickets and osteomalacia, defects of mineralization that differ from the loss of bone mass in osteoporosis.
Gut hormones such as ghrelin signal hunger to the hypothalamus, and the gut absorbs the vitamin D, calcium, and magnesium these pathways need.

sections.title: Insulin and glucagon in the fed and fasting states

blocks.text: Insulin and glucagon act as a switch on fuel metabolism. After a meal, glucose and amino acids stimulate pancreatic beta cells to release insulin, while glucagon from alpha cells falls, so the high insulin to glucagon ratio favors storage. During fasting the ratio reverses and the liver releases glucose and ketones. The liver sees both hormones first through the portal vein, so it responds most strongly to the ratio.
How insulin signals storage

The insulin receptor is a receptor tyrosine kinase. Its activated beta subunits phosphorylate insulin receptor substrate (IRS) proteins, which activate phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) and then Akt (protein kinase B). In skeletal muscle and adipose tissue, Akt signaling moves GLUT4 transporters from intracellular vesicles to the plasma membrane, which is the main way insulin lowers blood glucose. Liver (GLUT2), brain, and red cells take up glucose without insulin. Insulin also activates phosphodiesterase 3B, which lowers cAMP, and protein phosphatase 1, which removes the phosphates that glucagon signaling added. Dephosphorylation activates glycogen synthase and acetyl-CoA carboxylase and inactivates glycogen phosphorylase and hormone-sensitive lipase, so fuel is stored rather than released.

Insulin also raises hepatic fructose-2,6-bisphosphate and induces glucokinase, which speed glycolysis, and the acetyl-CoA produced is used for fatty acid synthesis (lipogenesis). In adipose tissue insulin increases lipoprotein lipase on capillary endothelium so triglyceride from chylomicrons and VLDL is taken up and stored. Through mTOR signaling it increases protein synthesis and reduces proteolysis, and it stimulates Na+/K+-ATPase, shifting potassium into cells.
How glucagon signals release

Glucagon binds a Gs-coupled receptor, mainly on hepatocytes, raising cAMP and activating protein kinase A (PKA). PKA activates phosphorylase kinase and therefore glycogen phosphorylase while inactivating glycogen synthase. It phosphorylates the bifunctional enzyme PFK-2/fructose-2,6-bisphosphatase, so fructose-2,6-bisphosphate falls, slowing phosphofructokinase-1 and releasing fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase; with pyruvate kinase also inhibited and PEPCK induced, carbon flows toward glucose (gluconeogenesis). In the fasting state acetyl-CoA carboxylase is held phosphorylated and inactive (AMP-activated protein kinase is the main kinase), so malonyl-CoA falls and no longer inhibits CPT-1; fatty acids then enter mitochondria for beta-oxidation and ketogenesis.

Skeletal muscle has few glucagon receptors and lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so muscle glycogen fuels only the muscle itself and is mobilized by epinephrine and contraction, not glucagon. Lipolysis in adipose tissue is driven mainly by the fall in insulin together with catecholamines; glucagon contributes little in humans.

blocks.title: Insulin and glucagon on fuel metabolism
rows: Small effect; low insulin and catecholamines dominate
Hepatic amino acid uptake for gluconeogenesis
blocks.caption: Every storage pathway belongs to insulin and every release pathway to glucagon; phosphorylation by PKA generally favors release, dephosphorylation favors storage.

blocks.text: As fasting continues, the sources of blood glucose shift. Liver glycogen supplies most glucose for the first several hours and is largely used within about a day, after which gluconeogenesis from lactate, glycerol, and amino acids (especially alanine) dominates. Over days, rising ketone use by the brain spares muscle protein.

Ketogenesis is a normal fasting adaptation. When insulin is low, fatty acids reach the liver, are oxidized, and the resulting acetyl-CoA is packaged as ketone bodies that the brain, heart, and skeletal muscle can burn. In a healthy fast the remaining insulin limits lipolysis, so ketones rise only modestly. In diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), absolute insulin deficiency with glucagon excess removes that brake, and production far outruns use. DKA occurs mainly in type 1 diabetes because the residual insulin of type 2 diabetes is usually enough to restrain lipolysis, so type 2 diabetes more often presents with hyperosmolar hyperglycemia without major ketosis.

blocks.title: From insulin deficiency to anion gap acidosis
steps: Insulin absent; counterregulatory hormones high
Hormone-sensitive lipase releases fatty acids from adipose
Low malonyl-CoA frees CPT-1 in liver
Beta-oxidation floods mitochondria with acetyl-CoA and NADH
Oxaloacetate diverted; acetyl-CoA exceeds TCA cycle capacity
HMG-CoA pathway forms acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate
Ketoacids dissociate; H+ consumes bicarbonate
Unmeasured anions accumulate: anion gap rises
blocks.caption: Lipolysis supplies the substrate and glucagon opens the mitochondrial gate; the result is overproduction of ketoacids.

blocks.text: Why acetyl-CoA becomes ketones

Beta-oxidation generates acetyl-CoA faster than the TCA cycle can accept it. Oxaloacetate, which acetyl-CoA needs to enter the cycle as citrate, is drawn off into gluconeogenesis, and the high NADH to NAD+ ratio from beta-oxidation shifts the remainder to malate. Two acetyl-CoA condense to acetoacetyl-CoA, then mitochondrial HMG-CoA synthase (the rate-limiting step) and HMG-CoA lyase release acetoacetate. Beta-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase reduces much of it to beta-hydroxybutyrate using NADH, so in DKA beta-hydroxybutyrate exceeds acetoacetate several-fold. Some acetoacetate decarboxylates spontaneously to acetone, which is exhaled and gives a fruity breath odor. The liver cannot use ketones because it lacks succinyl-CoA:3-ketoacid CoA transferase (thiophorase), the enzyme that reactivates acetoacetate in extrahepatic tissues.
Why the acidosis has an anion gap

Acetoacetic and beta-hydroxybutyric acids are strong enough to dissociate almost completely at body pH. Each H+ released is buffered by bicarbonate, which falls, while the ketoacid anion stays in plasma unmeasured. Chloride does not rise to replace the lost bicarbonate, so the anion gap, calculated as Na+ minus (Cl- plus HCO3-), increases above its reference range of about 8 to 12 mEq/L. The fall in pH stimulates peripheral and central chemoreceptors, producing deep, rapid Kussmaul respiration that lowers PaCO2 as respiratory compensation.

blocks.title: Other manifestations of DKA and their mechanism
rows: Gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis increase while GLUT4 uptake falls
Filtered glucose exceeds tubular reabsorption, causing osmotic diuresis
Normal or high serum K+ with total body K+ deficit
K+ leaves cells without insulin and with hyperosmolality, then is lost in urine
Nitroprusside detects acetoacetate and acetone, not beta-hydroxybutyrate
blocks.caption: Volume depletion lowers GFR, which reduces renal excretion of glucose and ketoacids and worsens both.

blocks.title: Reading the labs in DKA
blocks.text: A 19-year-old has glucose 520 mg/dL, Na+ 132, Cl- 96, HCO3- 10 mEq/L, arterial pH 7.24, and PaCO2 24 mm Hg. The anion gap is 132 minus (96 plus 10), or 26 mEq/L, well above about 12, so an unmeasured anion has accumulated. Winter's formula predicts PaCO2 of 1.5 times 10 plus 8, or 23 plus or minus 2 mm Hg; the measured 24 shows appropriate respiratory compensation from Kussmaul breathing, not an added respiratory disorder. Serum K+ of 5.4 mEq/L reflects shift out of cells, not a body surplus.

blocks.predict: Why does a patient fasting for three days have ketosis without acidosis, while a patient with untreated type 1 diabetes develops severe acidosis?
blocks.explain: In fasting, residual insulin restrains lipolysis and ketone production stays roughly matched to use by brain and muscle, so bicarbonate buffering keeps up. With no insulin, lipolysis and ketogenesis are unrestrained, production far exceeds use, and bicarbonate is consumed faster than the kidney regenerates it.
blocks.check: The first paragraph and the DKA flow.

blocks.text: Thyroid hormones are iodinated tyrosines, so dietary iodine is a structural building block: T4 (thyroxine) carries four iodine atoms and T3 (triiodothyronine) three. Selenium is not part of the hormone but is required by the enzymes that activate and inactivate it. Iodine therefore limits how much hormone the gland can make, while selenium limits how much active T3 tissues can generate.

blocks.title: Steps of thyroid hormone synthesis
rows: Iodide trapping (2 Na+ with 1 I-), secondary active
Oxidation and organification onto tyrosines (MIT, DIT)
Thyroid peroxidase (TPO) with H2O2 from DUOX2
Coupling: DIT plus DIT forms T4; MIT plus DIT forms T3
Endocytosis and proteolysis; release of T4 and T3
Recycling of iodide from MIT and DIT
blocks.caption: TSH stimulates nearly every step through Gs and cAMP; the gland secretes mostly T4 with a smaller amount of T3.

blocks.text: Selenium and the deiodinases

Most circulating T3 is made outside the thyroid by removing one iodine from the outer ring of T4. The three iodothyronine deiodinases contain selenocysteine at the active site. Type 1 (liver, kidney, thyroid) and type 2 (brain, pituitary, brown fat, muscle) perform outer ring deiodination to make T3. Type 3 removes an inner ring iodine, converting T4 to inactive reverse T3 and T3 to T2. Because the pituitary thyrotroph makes its own T3 from T4 through type 2 deiodinase, TSH secretion tracks serum T4 closely. Selenium also forms the active site of glutathione peroxidases, which protect follicular cells from the hydrogen peroxide they generate for TPO. Severe selenium deficiency impairs T4 to T3 conversion and is also linked to Keshan disease, a cardiomyopathy.
Iodine deficiency and goiter

blocks.title: Iodine deficiency goiter
steps: Dietary iodine is inadequate
Thyroid makes less T4
Less negative feedback on hypothalamus and pituitary
TRH and TSH rise
Follicular cell hypertrophy and hyperplasia
Gland enlarges and traps iodide more efficiently
blocks.caption: The loop restores hormone output partly at the cost of a goiter, diffuse at first and often multinodular later.

blocks.text: When iodine is scarce, the gland adapts. TSH increases NIS expression and iodide clearance, a greater share of MIT relative to DIT shifts output toward T3, which needs less iodine, and peripheral type 2 deiodinase activity rises. Serum T4 is therefore typically low, T3 normal or near normal, and TSH high; many patients remain clinically euthyroid with a goiter. Deficiency during pregnancy deprives the fetal brain of maternal T4 before the fetal thyroid works, causing congenital hypothyroidism with intellectual disability, short stature, and deafness in its severe endemic form. Goitrogens such as thiocyanate from poorly processed cassava compete with iodide at NIS and worsen deficiency.
Excess iodine has an opposite, transient effect: a large load acutely inhibits organification (the Wolff-Chaikoff effect), and normal glands escape within days by reducing NIS expression.

blocks.predict: In iodine deficiency, why can T3 stay near normal while T4 is low?
blocks.explain: The gland shifts toward making MIT and T3, which uses three rather than four iodine atoms, and increased deiodinase activity converts more of the available T4 to T3.
blocks.check: The paragraph on adaptation to iodine deficiency.

blocks.text: Vitamin D is a prohormone. It becomes active only after two hydroxylations, and only the second is tightly regulated. Its active form, calcitriol, raises calcium and phosphate absorption so bone can be mineralized; without it, collagen matrix is laid down but not calcified.

blocks.title: Vitamin D activation
steps: UVB light converts 7-dehydrocholesterol in skin to previtamin D3
Body heat isomerizes previtamin D3 to cholecalciferol (D3)
Binding protein (skin D3) or chylomicrons (dietary D) carry it to liver
Hepatic 25-hydroxylase forms 25-hydroxyvitamin D (storage form)
Renal proximal tubule 1-alpha-hydroxylase forms calcitriol
Calcitriol binds the nuclear vitamin D receptor in target cells
blocks.caption: Hepatic 25-hydroxylation is driven by substrate supply; renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation is the regulated step.

blocks.text: Renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase is stimulated by PTH and by low serum phosphate, and hypocalcemia stimulates it indirectly through PTH. It is suppressed by calcitriol itself, by high phosphate, and by FGF23 from osteocytes; when calcitriol is not needed, 24-hydroxylase diverts 25-hydroxyvitamin D to inactive products. Because 25-hydroxyvitamin D circulates at high concentration with a half-life of about 2 to 3 weeks, it is the best measure of vitamin D status. Calcitriol, with a half-life of hours, can be normal or even high early in deficiency because rising PTH drives its synthesis.

Calcitriol acts through the vitamin D receptor, a nuclear receptor. In the intestine it induces the apical calcium channel TRPV6, the binding protein calbindin, and the basolateral Ca2+-ATPase, and it increases sodium-phosphate cotransport. In bone it supports mineralization by supplying calcium and phosphate and, at high levels, increases osteoblast RANKL expression to promote resorption. It also feeds back to suppress PTH gene transcription.
Deficiency: secondary hyperparathyroidism and failed mineralization

With too little vitamin D, intestinal calcium absorption falls and ionized calcium dips. The parathyroids respond with more PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism), which mobilizes calcium from bone and increases renal calcium reabsorption, so serum calcium is held low-normal. PTH also inhibits proximal tubule phosphate reabsorption, so phosphate is lost in urine and serum phosphate falls. The low calcium times phosphate product leaves newly formed osteoid unmineralized, and osteoblasts working against it raise alkaline phosphatase.

blocks.title: Deficiency at different ages and its laboratory pattern
rows: Failed mineralization of growth plate cartilage and osteoid
Failed mineralization of osteoid during remodeling
Bowed legs, rachitic rosary, widened wrists, frayed metaphyses, craniotabes, delayed growth
Diffuse bone pain, proximal muscle weakness, pseudofractures (Looser zones)
Low 25-hydroxyvitamin D; calcium low or low-normal; phosphate low; PTH high; alkaline phosphatase high
blocks.caption: Osteoporosis differs: bone mass is reduced but what remains is normally mineralized, and serum calcium, phosphate, and PTH are usually normal.

blocks.text: Causes follow the activation pathway: limited sun exposure, darker skin, or high latitude at the skin step; fat malabsorption for dietary vitamin D; severe liver disease or drugs that induce vitamin D catabolism; and chronic kidney disease, where lost 1-alpha-hydroxylase and phosphate retention raise PTH. The reverse also teaches the regulation: granulomas such as sarcoidosis express unregulated 1-alpha-hydroxylase and cause hypercalcemia with suppressed PTH.

blocks.title: Predicting labs from where the pathway fails
blocks.text: Nutritional deficiency: 25-hydroxyvitamin D low, calcitriol normal or high early, PTH high, phosphate low. Chronic kidney disease: 25-hydroxyvitamin D may be normal, but calcitriol is low because renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase is lost; PTH is high, and phosphate is high rather than low because the failing kidney cannot excrete it. Hereditary vitamin D receptor defect: calcitriol is very high because PTH keeps stimulating its synthesis and the receptor cannot respond. Sarcoidosis: calcitriol high from granulomas, calcium high, PTH suppressed. In each case, find the failed or overactive step, then follow PTH and phosphate from it.

Magnesium is mostly intracellular and in bone, with only about 1% in the extracellular fluid, so serum magnesium (reference about 1.7 to 2.2 mg/dL) can underestimate total body depletion. Mg2+ is a cofactor for ATP-dependent enzymes, including adenylyl cyclase, which explains much of its role in the parathyroid axis.

Magnesium has a graded effect on PTH. Mg2+ acts as a weak agonist at the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) on chief cells, so a mild or acute fall in magnesium can slightly increase PTH release, much as low calcium does. Severe depletion, usually below about 1 mg/dL, has the opposite effect and paradoxically suppresses secretion. The current explanation is that intracellular Mg2+ normally restrains the Gi and Gq signaling by which the CaSR inhibits PTH release; without it, the receptor pathway signals as if calcium were high, so PTH release is inhibited. Hypermagnesemia also suppresses PTH, through direct CaSR activation.

Severe depletion also causes end-organ resistance. The PTH receptor signals through Gs and adenylyl cyclase, and both cyclase activity and Mg-ATP substrate depend on magnesium, so bone and kidney respond poorly to whatever PTH is present. Renal calcitriol production falls as well, reducing intestinal calcium absorption.

blocks.title: Why calcium stays low in severe magnesium deficiency
steps: Severe intracellular Mg2+ depletion
CaSR signaling disinhibited; PTH secretion falls
Remaining PTH acts poorly on bone and kidney
Less bone calcium release and renal reabsorption
Calcitriol and gut calcium absorption fall
Hypocalcemia with low or inappropriately normal PTH
blocks.caption: Calcium given alone cannot correct the defect because the parathyroid signal and its effect both remain impaired.

blocks.text: Restoring magnesium reverses the secretory block quickly, and PTH rises within minutes, while bone and kidney responsiveness and serum calcium recover over days. Hypokalemia often coexists for a parallel reason: intracellular Mg2+ normally blocks outward K+ flow through renal ROMK channels, so depletion increases potassium secretion in the distal nephron.

blocks.title: Common causes of hypomagnesemia by mechanism
rows: Alcohol use disorder, malnutrition, chronic diarrhea, malabsorption
Loop and thiazide diuretics, aminoglycosides, cisplatin, amphotericin B, Gitelman syndrome
Refeeding after starvation, recovery after parathyroidectomy (hungry bone)
blocks.caption: Alcohol use disorder combines poor intake, gut loss, and renal wasting.

blocks.text: Manifestations reflect the combined low magnesium, calcium, and potassium: neuromuscular irritability with tremor, tetany, and positive Chvostek and Trousseau signs, seizures, and arrhythmias including torsades de pointes from a prolonged QT.

sections.title: Leptin, ghrelin, and the link from obesity to insulin resistance

blocks.text: Appetite and energy expenditure are integrated in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus, which lies next to the median eminence, where the blood-brain barrier is relatively permeable to circulating hormones. Two opposing neuron groups sit there. POMC/CART neurons cleave pro-opiomelanocortin to alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (alpha-MSH), which activates melanocortin 4 receptors (MC4R) in the paraventricular nucleus to reduce intake and increase energy expenditure. NPY/AgRP neurons release neuropeptide Y, which drives feeding, and agouti-related peptide, which blocks MC4R, and they also inhibit POMC neurons directly.

blocks.title: Leptin and ghrelin compared
rows: Adipocytes, in proportion to fat mass
Reflects long-term energy stores; falls with fasting
Rises before meals, falls after eating
Growth hormone secretagogue receptor (GHSR1a), after acylation
blocks.caption: Leptin is a slow signal of stored fat; ghrelin is a fast signal tied to meals. Gut hormones such as PYY and GLP-1 add short-term satiety.

blocks.title: Leptin signaling to the arcuate nucleus
steps: Fat mass rises; adipocytes secrete more leptin
Leptin reaches arcuate leptin receptors
POMC neurons activated; NPY/AgRP neurons inhibited
Alpha-MSH activates MC4R, AgRP no longer blocks it
Food intake falls; energy expenditure rises
blocks.caption: A fall in leptin during fasting runs the loop in reverse, increasing hunger and suppressing the reproductive axis.

blocks.text: Leptin resistance and common obesity

Congenital leptin deficiency is rare and causes extreme early obesity, hyperphagia, and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism; MC4R mutations are the most common single-gene cause of obesity. Common obesity is different: leptin is high in proportion to fat mass, but appetite is not suppressed. This leptin resistance reflects reduced leptin transport into the brain and impaired receptor signaling, with negative regulators such as SOCS3 and PTP1B dampening the JAK2-STAT3 pathway. Because the low-leptin signal is strong but the high-leptin signal is weak, the system defends against weight loss far better than against weight gain. Prader-Willi syndrome shows the ghrelin side: ghrelin levels are markedly elevated, accompanying insatiable hunger.
Visceral fat and insulin resistance

Visceral adipose tissue is more lipolytically active than subcutaneous fat and drains into the portal vein, so it delivers free fatty acids directly to the liver. Excess fatty acids raise hepatic gluconeogenesis and VLDL output, and in liver and muscle their intermediates, especially diacylglycerol, activate protein kinase C isoforms that phosphorylate IRS-1 on serine, blocking its tyrosine phosphorylation by the insulin receptor. Enlarged visceral adipocytes and infiltrating macrophages secrete TNF-alpha and IL-6, which activate JNK and IKK-beta and impair IRS signaling further. Visceral fat also secretes less adiponectin, which normally improves insulin sensitivity by activating AMP-activated protein kinase. The result is reduced GLUT4 translocation in muscle and failure to suppress hepatic glucose output, the core defects of type 2 diabetes and the metabolic syndrome.

blocks.predict: An obese patient has a very high serum leptin. Would giving more leptin reduce appetite?
blocks.explain: Usually not. Common obesity reflects leptin resistance, so the arcuate signaling pathway is already saturated or blunted; extra leptin adds little. Only congenital leptin deficiency responds strongly.

integration.text: Phosphorylation by PKA and dephosphorylation by insulin-activated phosphatases set the direction of liver metabolism, and DKA is what happens when that switch is stuck on release; the acid-base findings then follow from bicarbonate buffering, the anion gap, and respiratory compensation. Iodine, selenium, vitamin D, and magnesium show that endocrine pathways depend on nutrients at specific enzymatic steps, so a deficiency can be predicted from where the nutrient sits: iodine limits synthesis, selenium limits activation, vitamin D limits the mineral supply for bone, and magnesium limits both PTH release and its signaling.

Pathology and immunology complete the picture. Rickets and osteomalacia are mineralization failures, unlike osteoporosis, and granulomatous disease shows unregulated vitamin D activation. Visceral adiposity links the hypothalamic control of appetite to the cytokine-driven insulin resistance of type 2 diabetes. Limits: serum magnesium poorly reflects body stores, early calcitriol can be misleadingly normal, and reference ranges vary by laboratory, so each value is read alongside PTH, phosphate, and the clinical setting.

summary: Insulin, through PI3K-Akt and dephosphorylation, stores fuel: GLUT4 uptake, glycogen synthesis, glycolysis, lipogenesis, and protein synthesis.
Glucagon, through cAMP and PKA in the liver, releases fuel: glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis via lower fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, and ketogenesis via lower malonyl-CoA.
In DKA, unrestrained lipolysis and an open CPT-1 gate overload liver mitochondria with acetyl-CoA, which becomes acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate.
Ketoacids consume bicarbonate and leave unmeasured anions, giving an anion gap metabolic acidosis with Kussmaul respiration and a total body potassium deficit.
Iodine is built into T4 and T3; deficiency lowers T4, raises TSH, and causes goiter, while selenium-containing deiodinases convert T4 to T3.
Vitamin D is activated in skin, liver, and kidney; renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase is the regulated step, stimulated by PTH and low phosphate.
Vitamin D deficiency causes secondary hyperparathyroidism, low phosphate, high alkaline phosphatase, and unmineralized osteoid: rickets in children, osteomalacia in adults.
Severe hypomagnesemia suppresses PTH secretion and blunts its action, so hypocalcemia persists until magnesium is restored.
Leptin from fat activates POMC and inhibits NPY/AgRP neurons to cause satiety; ghrelin from the stomach stimulates NPY/AgRP to cause hunger.
Common obesity shows high leptin with leptin resistance, and visceral fat drives insulin resistance through portal fatty acids, inflammatory cytokines, and low adiponectin.

verify: Duration of hepatic glycogen supply in fasting is quoted from about 12 to 24 hours or more; this chapter says largely used within about a day.
Anion gap reference range depends on the laboratory method (about 8 to 12 mEq/L classically, lower with modern analyzers); confirm the range NABNE uses.
Diagnostic thresholds for DKA (for example glucose above 250 mg/dL, pH below 7.30, bicarbonate below 18 mEq/L) differ between guidelines and were not stated as fact here.

The mechanism by which severe hypomagnesemia suppresses PTH (disinhibition of CaSR G protein signaling) is a current model; older sources describe only a Mg-dependent secretory step. The threshold of about 1 mg/dL varies by source.
Serum magnesium reference range is about 1.7 to 2.2 mg/dL in many laboratories; some use 1.5 to 2.4 mg/dL.
25-hydroxyvitamin D cutoffs for deficiency (often below 20 ng/mL, or 50 nmol/L) and its half-life of about 2 to 3 weeks vary among sources.
Confirm whether NABNE expects the eponyms Wolff-Chaikoff, Keshan disease, and Looser zones, or only the descriptive terms.
